articles.title: This Is the Most Popular Thanksgiving Dessert in Each State—Did Your Favorite Nab the Top Spot?
articles.content:
In my family, Thanksgiving rules. For the past 30-plus years, my brother, sister, mom and I pick a place we can all get to from our far-flung locations, and we meet up to cook a traditional Thanksgiving spread. Well, I cook, and the rest of the clan lounges around drinking coffee and watching the Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade.
I’ve made a Thanksgiving turkey in a tiny Philadelphia galley kitchen, a green bean casserole at a log cabin in the Ozarks and mashed potatoes and gravy at several random Las Vegas timeshares and Airbnbs (we took a cab to the grocery store one year). But no matter how terrible the kitchen utensils are, I always make a pumpkin pie, an apple pie and, lately, a pecan pie too.
This Thanksgiving trifecta of dessert pies covers everyone’s bases—especially mine, since I hate pumpkin pie and practically get the apple pie all to myself. What about you? Do you cook (or buy, no shame) a traditional after-turkey-dinner treat, or does your family like something a little more off the beaten path? DoorDash decided to answer this question for families across the nation, and coming up, we have the surprising answers.
Read on to discover which Thanksgiving desserts are tops nationally, as well as state by state, and get ready to dig in.
Get Reader’s Digest’s Read Up newsletter for more food, holidays, humor, travel and fun facts all week long.
DoorDash looked at orders between Nov. 19 and Nov. 27, 2025, to see just what sweets Americans were hungry for on Thanksgiving. Compiling data from retail, restaurant and grocery-store DoorDash orders, they compared national trends with state data to determine how traditional Thanksgiving desserts like pumpkin, pecan and apple pies fared next to up-and-comers like cake.
The results are literally all over the map here, with pumpkin pie rubbing shoulders with other dessert giants more commonly seen at your kid’s birthday party. Here’s how the data shook out.
Traditional Thanksgiving-dessert lovers can rest easy, because pumpkin pie came out on top in 14 states, or more than a quarter (28%) of the country. Other fall-flavored pies scored as well, with pecan pie winning four states and apple pie three. But as you’ll see below, some interesting nontraditional dessert trends appear to be gaining steam.
If you’ve ever woken from your post-turkey nap craving chocolate instead of pumpkin pie, you have plenty of company. In the national rankings, chocolate cake was the most-ordered dessert during DoorDash’s Thanksgiving buying period, knocking pumpkin pie all the way down to fourth. Apple pie ranked second, while cheesecake (?) sat comfortably in third.
Could Thanksgiving become a major chocolate-themed holiday? All signs point to yes. In addition to the overwhelming national win, chocolate cake won five individual states. Meanwhile, chocolate pie was tops in six states and made the national list at No. 6 overall.
Move over, Rust Belt, because you will henceforth be called the Cheesecake Belt. Eight states, from West Virginia and Ohio all the way over to the Midwestern states of Minnesota and Iowa, sat down to cheesecake for Thanksgiving last year. Wisconsin was the lone pumpkin-pie holdout in the entire region, which is a little surprising given its fame as America’s Dairyland.
The West also showed up big for pumpkin pie. Aside from Wisconsin, every state that went for pumpkin pie—13 out of 14—is west of the Mississippi River. Pecan pie stuck to its Southern roots, winning in Texas, Oklahoma, Louisiana and Tennessee, while apple pie’s three wins came (appropriately) in New York as well as Massachusetts and Connecticut.
Let’s talk about pound cake. This old-fashioned, dense buttery cake turned up as the top dessert choice for Thanksgiving in an astounding six states, more popular than both apple and pecan pie. It also made the top five nationally. If it seems like a strange choice for not only Thanksgiving but just in general, half a dozen states and your grandmother would like a word.
We already talked about chocolate cake, but its birthday-and-wedding partner in crime, vanilla cake, also did surprisingly well in DoorDash’s annual Thanksgiving report. It won three states in the coastal Atlantic region: Virginia, North Carolina and South Carolina.
Finally, Georgia went way out on a limb this year, and that limb belongs to a Key lime tree. The tart, custardy Key lime pie was the No. 1 most popular Thanksgiving dessert in the Peach State—a place where Key limes only grow with some help because they do not fare well in Georgia winters.

Which Thanksgiving dessert earned the No. 1 spot in the most states?

Traditional Thanksgiving-dessert lovers can rest easy, because pumpkin pie came out on top in 14 states, or more than a quarter (28%) of the country. The West also showed up big for pumpkin pie. Aside from Wisconsin, every state that went for pumpkin pie—13 out of 14—is west of the Mississippi River. Pecan pie stuck to its Southern roots, winning in Texas, Oklahoma, Louisiana and Tennessee, while apple pie’s three wins came (appropriately) in New York as well as Massachusetts and Connecticut.

Were there any other big surprises?

Let’s talk about pound cake. This old-fashioned, dense buttery cake turned up as the top dessert choice for Thanksgiving in an astounding six states, more popular than both apple and pecan pie. articles.title: Watch The Reader’s Digest Escalator Interview with Actor and Author Tony Shalhoub
articles.content: Whether you know him as the lovable, obsessive-compulsive detective Adrian Monk from Monk, the hilariously opinionated Abe Weissman from The Marvelous Mrs. Maisel or from big-screen favorites like Big Night, Men in Black and Galaxy Quest, chances are Tony Shalhoub has made you laugh at least once (and probably a whole lot more). With a career spanning more than four decades, the beloved actor has earned four Emmy Awards, a Golden Globe and a Tony Award for his Broadway performance in The Band’s Visit. Now, he’s adding another title to his impressive résumé: author. And this time, the stories he’s telling hit a little closer to home. For this episode of The Reader’s Digest Escalator Interview, we caught up with Shalhoub to talk about his new book, We Thought They’d Never Leave: Musings on Food and Family, co-written with his daughter, Josie Adams. Part love letter to family culinary traditions (with 20 original recipes included for good measure) and part personal narrative, the book takes readers inside the Shalhoub family’s famously large gatherings in Wisconsin. “A lot of it is about the family reunion that we have every year, that we’ve had for the last 50-odd years,” Shalhoub tells us. “The numbers have grown to ridiculous size.” But family stories are just the appetizer. Shalhoub also reveals what he’s currently reading, some of his favorite authors and one hilariously specific thing he’s particular about in real life. And that’s not all he had to share. articles.title: We Just Got an Update on Punch the Monkey—And It’s the Best News You’ll Hear All Week
articles.content:
Punch the Monkey is back in the news, and if you’ve been worried about how the little guy is faring, you’re going to love this update. For the uninitiated, Punch the Monkey is a Japanese macaque, or snow monkey, who was abandoned by his mother and became an internet sensation earlier this year.
Zookeepers at the Ichikawa City Zoo and Botanical Gardens, where Punch was born, hand-reared him from birth, famously giving him a plush orangutan from Ikea that he sweetly cuddled with and toted around his enclosure. It’s been a series of highs and lows ever since. At first, he was rejected and seemingly bullied by the other “mean” monkeys. It was heartbreaking. Then, he was slowly but surely accepted into the fold. (Hooray!)
Now, the zoo is sharing a video that is once again making the internet go wild for Punch the Monkey and his dedicated caregivers. Read on to see the latest footage of the adorable little monkey, and get ready to say, “Awwww.”
Get Reader’s Digest’s Read Up newsletter for more news, animals, tech, humor, travel and fun facts all week long.
飼育員撮影、本日のパンチです。
パンチや他の個体の様子は日々変化します。
観察したり交流しながらケアをしたり、
季節や天候にあわせた給餌の調整も。
こうした飼育員の対応があるからこそ、
パンチは元気に暮らしていると思います。
そんな飼育員たちにも応援をお願いします。
#市川市動植物園 https://t.co/5KMyw50Jpn
— 市川市動植物園（公式） (@ichikawa_zoo) November 8, 2026
On Nov. 8, the Ichikawa City Zoo posted a sweet update featuring Punch and another small macaque roughhousing in their enclosure. The duo wrestle and tackle each other, periodically grabbing onto a green rope before a larger macaque climbs up to interrupt their play.
We don’t know who this buzzkill is, but the playful youngsters immediately turn their attention to the interloper before engaging in some mutual grooming. It’s definitely the cutest thing I’ve seen since … the last time Punch took the internet by storm.
To no one’s surprise, the internet is going wild over the latest Punch update.
That was the rumor, though a zookeeper declined to confirm this gossip to ABC News. Here’s what happened: Back in April, the Ichikawa City Zoo shared a video that showed Punch and another young monkey cuddling. Fans immediately dubbed the new pal a girlfriend, but the head of the zoo, Takashi Yasunaga, said he was “unsure” if that was what was really going on, stressing that the footage indicated that other monkeys were increasingly warming to Punch.
He appears to be living his best monkey life—playing, climbing, grooming and making friends. “Punch’s behavior, along with that of the other monkeys, changes from day to day,” the Ichikawa City Zoo said in the X post. Earlier this year, the zoo reported that it had temporarily removed a few aggressive troop members, but right now, things appear to being going well.
The zoo also gave a shout-out to its staff, who interact with Punch and other animals as they feed and nurture them: “We believe Punch is able to live a healthy, happy life because of the care and attention provided by these zookeepers,” the post reads. So, as you squee over Punch and his new friends, remember who made all this possible: “Please show your support for the keepers too.”

articles.title: 5 Signs Your Thrift-Shop Furniture Find Is Actually Valuable—And a Great Deal
articles.content:
Few things compare to the thrill of finding a hidden gem at a thrift store. One minute, you’re browsing a jumble of junk, and the next, you’ve struck gold with a stunning vintage piece—at a fraction of what you’d pay for something new. Maybe it’s an Art Deco dresser with the coolest inlaid-wood waterfall design. Maybe it’s a curved Mid-century Modern sofa that looks like it belongs on a movie set. Or maybe it’s something a lot more modern that you just really, really love. Score! It can honestly be hard to believe that some of these items were given away. What were these people thinking?
Well, we’re glad they were thinking they’d donate these items instead of tossing them in the trash! Thrifting has skyrocketed in popularity lately, as shoppers look to save money and prioritize sustainable choices. And with more Baby Boomers downsizing, there’s a surge of well-made, older furniture finding its way into secondhand shops. In fact, people are calling this the Golden Age of Thrifting, and it’s exciting as it sounds—if you do it right. So how can you tell a true find from an old piece that’s simply seen better days? Knowing what to look for can help you spot quality craftsmanship, recognize furniture styles from different eras and avoid overpaying.
To uncover the secrets of buying secondhand furniture, we spoke with Danielle Sandusky, co-owner of Modern Bungalow, an award-winning furniture boutique known for American-made, Amish-built, solid-wood items. You’ll definitely want to read this before your next thrifting expedition!
Get Reader’s Digest’s Read Up newsletter for more shopping, money, knowledge, humor, cleaning and fun facts all week long.
In many cases, older furniture was built with stronger, more substantial materials and better construction techniques than today’s mass-produced alternatives. There’s a good reason people say “They don’t make ’em like they used to.” However, age alone doesn’t guarantee quality. A well-made modern piece can be just as durable as a vintage one, and some older furniture was never particularly well made to begin with.
One reason older furniture can feel different is the way it was manufactured. Before large-scale industrial production became widespread, many furniture makers relied on skilled craftspeople and hands-on construction methods. Industrialization, of course, dramatically changed things with engineered wood, particleboard, laminates and other lower-cost materials. “Mass-produced furniture is carefully designed to look good in photos and from just one angle,” Sandusky explains. “If you start pulling out drawers and opening doors and it looks different than you expected, it’s because the company likely skimped on materials.”
Fortunately, quality craftsmanship hasn’t disappeared. There are still furniture makers producing solid-wood pieces with traditional joinery and durable construction. The key is learning to recognize those qualities, whether you’re shopping for something decades old or something brand new.
Before falling in love with a thrift-store find, take the time to examine how it was made. Here’s what can tell you more about an item’s quality than its appearance alone.
One of the easiest ways to get an initial sense of an item’s construction is to pick it up or gently test its stability. Solid hardwood furniture generally has some heft, while lightweight construction can indicate the use of thinner materials or hollow components. Sandusky also recommends pushing gently on a corner to see whether the entire piece wobbles. A sturdy dresser, table or cabinet shouldn’t feel like it’s about to come apart when you touch it.
For upholstered furniture, pay attention to the frame. Push down on the back and arms, and check whether they feel solid or hollow. If the frame bows, feels squishy or seems unstable, it may not have strong structural support. Alarm bells should also go off if you notice sagging cushions or wooden corners poking through the fabric.
The type of wood used in a piece of furniture can make a significant difference in its durability. Sandusky recommends familiarizing yourself with the grain patterns of hardwoods such as maple, cherry, oak and walnut. These denser, heavier woods are valued for their strength and appearance.
Look closely at the underside, back and edges of a piece to get a better idea what it’s made from. Can you identify the wood grain? Does the material look consistent throughout, or does it appear to be a thin decorative layer covering another material?
Sandusky suggests paying particular attention to the underside of wooden tables. A surface that is rough, unfinished or splintery may indicate that the maker didn’t put much care into the construction. You can also gently press a fingernail against an inconspicuous area to get a sense of the wood’s density.
Dovetail joints are one of the classic signs of quality furniture construction. These interlocking, wedge-shaped joints connect the sides of a drawer to its front and back, helping hold the pieces together without relying solely on nails or screws.
You’ll typically find dovetail joints at the corners of wooden drawers. They’re worth looking for in older furniture, particularly dressers, desks and cabinets. But don’t stop at the front of the drawer. Sandusky cautions that some manufacturers use dovetail joints only on the front corners to give the appearance of quality construction. Sneaky! So pull the drawer all the way out and inspect the back corners too.
Ideally, the drawer box should also be made from solid wood rather than plywood or another inexpensive material. These details can help distinguish a genuinely well-constructed piece from one designed to look more expensive than it is.
A manufacturer’s label, stamp, signature or other identifying mark can offer valuable clues about an item’s age and origin. Check the back, inside the drawers and even the bottom of cabinets for identifying information. A maker’s mark may help you determine who produced the furniture, when it was made and whether it belongs to a recognizable design collection. This can be especially useful when researching pieces from established furniture makers or well-known designers.
However, a missing label doesn’t automatically mean an older piece isn’t valuable. Many older furnishings were never marked, and identifying information can disappear over time. Think of a maker’s mark as a helpful starting point rather than a requirement.
Even a beautifully constructed piece can become a money pit if it needs extensive repairs. Before purchasing, inspect the furniture carefully, including areas that aren’t immediately visible. Watch out for structural damage, loose joints, water damage, warped wood, significant cracks and evidence of previous repairs. Check that drawers slide properly and cabinet doors open and close without difficulty.
The good news is that not every imperfection is a deal-breaker. Sandusky says surface scratches, worn hardware, sticky drawers and slightly crooked doors are often relatively easy to address. A little cleaning, a touch-up kit or replacement hardware may be all a piece needs. However, she warns shoppers not to underestimate the cost and difficulty of refinishing an entire piece of furniture. Stripping old finishes, repairing damaged wood and applying a new finish can require considerable time, skill and money.
When in doubt, distinguish between cosmetic imperfections and problems that affect the furniture’s structural integrity. The former may be an opportunity, while the latter could turn an inexpensive purchase into an expensive project.
Recognizing popular furniture styles can help you narrow down when a piece was made and what details to look for. Although styles sometimes overlap, certain materials, silhouettes and decorative elements are closely associated with particular periods.
Here are some of the major furniture eras and the features you might encounter while thrifting—or even find in your grandma’s attic.

As Sandusky points out, the idea of collectible furniture can sometimes distract shoppers from what matters most when furnishing a home. “Collectible styles imply that you should expect it to grow in value,” she says. “That’s true for very iconic pieces, but for most of our homes, we generally aren’t looking to ‘collect.’ We simply want to furnish our lives.” In other words, don’t overlook a well-made, beautifully designed piece just because you can’t identify its exact era.
You don’t have to become an antique-furniture expert to make smarter thrift-store purchases. A few digital tools and reference resources can help you identify unfamiliar pieces and decide whether they’re worth a closer look.
A good deal isn’t necessarily the piece with the lowest price tag. Consider the quality of the furniture’s construction, its overall condition, the amount of work it needs and how much comparable pieces are actually selling for. Begin by comparing the asking price with similar items from the same maker, period or style. Look at completed sales rather than relying exclusively on current listings, since sellers can ask for just about anything for a vintage dresser or dining table.
Next, factor in the cost of any repairs or improvements. A sturdy wooden table with a few surface scratches may be an excellent purchase, especially if it only needs a little cleaning or polishing. But a piece with extensive water damage, broken structural joints or a finish that needs to be completely stripped and replaced may cost considerably more than its original price suggests.
Also keep in mind the furniture’s practical value. Will it fit in your home? Does it serve a purpose? Does it fit well with your existing furniture? Is it something you’ll enjoy using for years? A beautifully constructed piece that you’ll actually use may be a better investment in your home than an expensive collectible that doesn’t suit your needs.
And remember that resale value and personal value aren’t always the same thing. Even a piece that isn’t particularly rare or collectible can be worth purchasing if it’s well made, reasonably priced and you absolutely love it. Sandusky’s advice is refreshingly simple: “If it’s well made and makes your heart sing, grab it!”
Sandusky encourages shoppers to think about the experience of furnishing a home rather than approaching every purchase as an investment. “Don’t buy to flip,” she says. “Buy to make your home feel collected and cozy—full of the work of craftspeople grateful to you for giving their labor a second life.”
That’s perhaps the best part of shopping for secondhand furniture. You’re not just finding something to fill an empty corner. You’re giving a well-made piece another chapter and potentially bringing home something you’ll treasure for years to come.

Few things compare to the thrill of finding a hidden gem at a thrift store. One minute, you’re browsing a jumble of junk, and the next, you’ve struck gold with a stunning vintage piece—at a fraction of what you’d pay for something new. Maybe it’s an Art Deco dresser with the coolest inlaid-wood waterfall design. Maybe it’s a curved Mid-century Modern sofa that looks like it belongs on a movie set. Or maybe it’s something a lot more modern that you just really, really love. Score! It can honestly be hard to believe that some of these items were given away. What were these people thinking?

Well, we’re glad they were thinking they’d donate these items instead of tossing them in the trash! Thrifting has skyrocketed in popularity lately, as shoppers look to save money and prioritize sustainable choices. And with more Baby Boomers downsizing, there’s a surge of well-made, older furniture finding its way into secondhand shops. In fact, people are calling this the Golden Age of Thrifting, and it’s exciting as it sounds—if you do it right. So how can you tell a true find from an old piece that’s simply seen better days? Knowing what to look for can help you spot quality craftsmanship, recognize furniture styles from different eras and avoid overpaying.

To uncover the secrets of buying secondhand furniture, we spoke with Danielle Sandusky, co-owner of Modern Bungalow, an award-winning furniture boutique known for American-made, Amish-built, solid-wood items. You’ll definitely want to read this before your next thrifting expedition!

Get Reader’s Digest’s Read Up newsletter for more shopping, money, knowledge, humor, cleaning and fun facts all week long.

Is old furniture really made better than the new stuff?

In many cases, older furniture was built with stronger, more substantial materials and better construction techniques than today’s mass-produced alternatives. There’s a good reason people say “They don’t make ’em like they used to.” However, age alone doesn’t guarantee quality. A well-made modern piece can be just as durable as a vintage one, and some older furniture was never particularly well made to begin with.

One reason older furniture can feel different is the way it was manufactured. Before large-scale industrial production became widespread, many furniture makers relied on skilled craftspeople and hands-on construction methods. Industrialization, of course, dramatically changed things with engineered wood, particleboard, laminates and other lower-cost materials. “Mass-produced furniture is carefully designed to look good in photos and from just one angle,” Sandusky explains. “If you start pulling out drawers and opening doors and it looks different than you expected, it’s because the company likely skimped on materials.”

Fortunately, quality craftsmanship hasn’t disappeared. There are still furniture makers producing solid-wood pieces with traditional joinery and durable construction. The key is learning to recognize those qualities, whether you’re shopping for something decades old or something brand new.

What questions should you ask yourself when looking at an old piece of furniture?

Before falling in love with a thrift-store find, take the time to examine how it was made. Here’s what can tell you more about an item’s quality than its appearance alone.

1. Is it heavy and sturdy?

One of the easiest ways to get an initial sense of an item’s construction is to pick it up or gently test its stability. Solid hardwood furniture generally has some heft, while lightweight construction can indicate the use of thinner materials or hollow components. Sandusky also recommends pushing gently on a corner to see whether the entire piece wobbles. A sturdy dresser, table or cabinet shouldn’t feel like it’s about to come apart when you touch it.

For upholstered furniture, pay attention to the frame. Push down on the back and arms, and check whether they feel solid or hollow. If the frame bows, feels squishy or seems unstable, it may not have strong structural support. Alarm bells should also go off if you notice sagging cushions or wooden corners poking through the fabric.

2. Is it made from solid hardwood?

The type of wood used in a piece of furniture can make a significant difference in its durability. Sandusky recommends familiarizing yourself with the grain patterns of hardwoods such as maple, cherry, oak and walnut. These denser, heavier woods are valued for their strength and appearance.

Look closely at the underside, back and edges of a piece to get a better idea what it’s made from. Can you identify the wood grain? Does the material look consistent throughout, or does it appear to be a thin decorative layer covering another material?

Sandusky suggests paying particular attention to the underside of wooden tables. A surface that is rough, unfinished or splintery may indicate that the maker didn’t put much care into the construction. You can also gently press a fingernail against an inconspicuous area to get a sense of the wood’s density.

3. Are the drawers built with dovetail joints?

Dovetail joints are one of the classic signs of quality furniture construction. These interlocking, wedge-shaped joints connect the sides of a drawer to its front and back, helping hold the pieces together without relying solely on nails or screws.

You’ll typically find dovetail joints at the corners of wooden drawers. They’re worth looking for in older furniture, particularly dressers, desks and cabinets. But don’t stop at the front of the drawer. Sandusky cautions that some manufacturers use dovetail joints only on the front corners to give the appearance of quality construction. Sneaky! So pull the drawer all the way out and inspect the back corners too.

Ideally, the drawer box should also be made from solid wood rather than plywood or another inexpensive material. These details can help distinguish a genuinely well-constructed piece from one designed to look more expensive than it is.

4. Can you find a maker’s mark or label?

A manufacturer’s label, stamp, signature or other identifying mark can offer valuable clues about an item’s age and origin. Check the back, inside the drawers and even the bottom of cabinets for identifying information. A maker’s mark may help you determine who produced the furniture, when it was made and whether it belongs to a recognizable design collection. This can be especially useful when researching pieces from established furniture makers or well-known designers.

However, a missing label doesn’t automatically mean an older piece isn’t valuable. Many older furnishings were never marked, and identifying information can disappear over time. Think of a maker’s mark as a helpful starting point rather than a requirement.

5. What kind of condition is it in?

Even a beautifully constructed piece can become a money pit if it needs extensive repairs. Before purchasing, inspect the furniture carefully, including areas that aren’t immediately visible. Watch out for structural damage, loose joints, water damage, warped wood, significant cracks and evidence of previous repairs. Check that drawers slide properly and cabinet doors open and close without difficulty.

The good news is that not every imperfection is a deal-breaker. Sandusky says surface scratches, worn hardware, sticky drawers and slightly crooked doors are often relatively easy to address. A little cleaning, a touch-up kit or replacement hardware may be all a piece needs. However, she warns shoppers not to underestimate the cost and difficulty of refinishing an entire piece of furniture. Stripping old finishes, repairing damaged wood and applying a new finish can require considerable time, skill and money.

When in doubt, distinguish between cosmetic imperfections and problems that affect the furniture’s structural integrity. The former may be an opportunity, while the latter could turn an inexpensive purchase into an expensive project.

How can you identify old furniture by era?

Recognizing popular furniture styles can help you narrow down when a piece was made and what details to look for. Although styles sometimes overlap, certain materials, silhouettes and decorative elements are closely associated with particular periods.

Here are some of the major furniture eras and the features you might encounter while thrifting—or even find in your grandma’s attic.

  • Victorian (1837–1900s): Victorian furniture is often ornate, substantial and decorative, reflecting the period’s taste for elaborate interiors. Look for dark woods, intricate carvings, curved lines, button-tufted upholstery, marble tops and decorative hardware. Popular pieces included elaborate bedroom sets, carved parlor chairs, sideboards, dressers and occasional tables. Not every Victorian piece is especially valuable, but well-preserved examples with distinctive craftsmanship can be worth investigating.
  • Arts and Crafts (1880–1920s): A reaction against the ornamentation and mass production associated with industrialization, the Arts and Crafts movement emphasized simplicity and skilled craftsmanship. Furniture often features sturdy oak construction, straight lines, exposed joinery and understated hardware. Mission-style chairs, bookcases, desks, dining tables and sideboards are common examples. 
  • Art Nouveau (1890–1910s): Art Nouveau furniture is recognizable for its flowing, organic lines inspired by nature. Think curved silhouettes, asymmetrical designs, floral motifs, vines, leaves and decorative inlays. Some pieces incorporate stained glass, intricate wood carving and unusual hardware. Cabinets, display cases, chairs and dressing tables are among the furniture forms associated with the style.
  • Art Deco (1920–1930s): Art Deco brought a more glamorous, streamlined aesthetic to furniture design. Look for geometric patterns, symmetrical shapes, rounded corners, stepped silhouettes, mirrored surfaces and high-gloss finishes. Exotic woods and decorative veneers, including walnut and Macassar ebony, were popular. Waterfall dressers and vanities, club chairs, slipper chairs, cocktail cabinets and sleek bedroom furniture are particularly recognizable examples.
  • Mid-century Modern (1945–1970s): Mid-century Modern (or MCM) furniture remains popular today for its clean lines, functional designs and relatively simple silhouettes. Search for details like tapered legs, organic curves, low profiles, streamlined wooden cabinets and a combination of wood, metal and molded materials. Teak, walnut and other warm-toned woods are common. Credenzas, dining sets, lounge chairs, coffee tables and compact bedroom furniture are especially recognizable finds. 

One important distinction: A piece doesn’t have to belong to a famous design era to be worth purchasing. As Sandusky points out, the idea of collectible furniture can sometimes distract shoppers from what matters most when furnishing a home. “Collectible styles imply that you should expect it to grow in value,” she says. “That’s true for very iconic pieces, but for most of our homes, we generally aren’t looking to ‘collect.’ We simply want to furnish our lives.” In other words, don’t overlook a well-made, beautifully designed piece just because you can’t identify its exact era.

How can you get a little extra help with this?

You don’t have to become an antique-furniture expert to make smarter thrift-store purchases. A few digital tools and reference resources can help you identify unfamiliar pieces and decide whether they’re worth a closer look.

  • Start with Google Lens. If you spot an unusual dresser, chair or table, take a photo and use Google Lens to search for visually similar pieces. A reverse image search can help you identify a style, discover a potential manufacturer or find useful terms for further research. You can also photograph a maker’s label or stamp to see whether it matches a known furniture brand. Just remember that similar-looking pieces aren’t necessarily authentic originals.
  • Look up past sales with WorthPoint. If you suspect you’ve found something particularly interesting, WorthPoint offers a database of historical auction and marketplace sales, along with research tools for identifying makers’ marks and other collectibles. Its more extensive research features require a subscription, but it can be useful for shoppers who regularly visit antique stores, estate sales and thrift shops.
  • Browse auction and resale listings. Websites such as eBay, LiveAuctioneers and Chairish can help you find comparable furniture and learn more about particular styles, makers and designs. Pay particular attention to completed or sold listings when available—an asking price isn’t necessarily what someone is willing to pay.
  • Consult an antiques or furniture specialist. If a piece has an unusual maker’s mark, distinctive construction or a potentially important design history, consider asking an experienced antiques dealer, furniture restorer or qualified appraiser for help. Bring clear photographs of the front, back, underside, drawers, hardware and any identifying marks. If you’re considering a substantial purchase, an in-person inspection is even better.

Once you’ve determined an item is good quality, how can you determine if it’s a good deal?

A good deal isn’t necessarily the piece with the lowest price tag. Consider the quality of the furniture’s construction, its overall condition, the amount of work it needs and how much comparable pieces are actually selling for. Begin by comparing the asking price with similar items from the same maker, period or style. Look at completed sales rather than relying exclusively on current listings, since sellers can ask for just about anything for a vintage dresser or dining table.

Next, factor in the cost of any repairs or improvements. A sturdy wooden table with a few surface scratches may be an excellent purchase, especially if it only needs a little cleaning or polishing. But a piece with extensive water damage, broken structural joints or a finish that needs to be completely stripped and replaced may cost considerably more than its original price suggests.

Also keep in mind the furniture’s practical value. Will it fit in your home? Does it serve a purpose? Does it fit well with your existing furniture? Is it something you’ll enjoy using for years? A beautifully constructed piece that you’ll actually use may be a better investment in your home than an expensive collectible that doesn’t suit your needs.

And remember that resale value and personal value aren’t always the same thing. Even a piece that isn’t particularly rare or collectible can be worth purchasing if it’s well made, reasonably priced and you absolutely love it. Sandusky’s advice is refreshingly simple: “If it’s well made and makes your heart sing, grab it!”

What else should you keep in mind when thrifting?

Sandusky encourages shoppers to think about the experience of furnishing a home rather than approaching every purchase as an investment. “Don’t buy to flip,” she says. “Buy to make your home feel collected and cozy—full of the work of craftspeople grateful to you for giving their labor a second life.”

That’s perhaps the best part of shopping for secondhand furniture. You’re not just finding something to fill an empty corner. You’re giving a well-made piece another chapter and potentially bringing home something you’ll treasure for years to come.

articles.title: This Hidden iPhone Feature Will Make Holiday Cooking and Baking a Million Times Easier
articles.content:
Picture it: You’re making holiday cookies, up to your elbows in flour and sugar and little red and green sprinkles, when your recipe throws you for a loop. In the old days, you might have just muddled through and hoped for the best, or searched the back of your cookbook for tips and tricks to solve whatever problem you’d encountered.
But now, you’re more likely to reach for your iPhone, which is probably what you’re using to follow the recipe anyway. iPhones have changed the way we cook and bake, and I can’t tell you how many times I’ve reached for mine to Google something mid-recipe. But what if you didn’t have to search the internet at all?
Good news: You don’t, at least for one particularly common cooking problem—because the answer is right on your phone. Ahead, I’ll tell you about a super handy iPhone feature that I had no idea existed until recently but is guaranteed to make my holiday cooking and yours so much easier.
Read on to learn about this secret iPhone feature, and get baking!
Get Reader’s Digest’s Read Up newsletter for more holidays, tech, travel, entertainment, humor and fun facts all week long.
It’s the Unit Conversion feature in your iPhone’s calculator, and it really helps. Need to know how many grams are in an ounce or how many pints there are in a quart? This little feature can tell you. Does your Nigella Lawson turkey recipe call for liters of brine instead of gallons? Grab your iPhone calculator and make that turkey with confidence.
I cook a lot, but aside from a handful of familiar conversions, like 3 teaspoons = 1 tablespoon, my brain just doesn’t have a lot of room for math-y minutiae. Just the other day, a recipe called for 8 tablespoons of water, and I got out a cup, filled it to the top and counted them out. Another wanted me to add a “dram” of flavoring, which might as well have been in a different language, not to mention from another century.
Little did I know that 8 tablespoons is a half-cup, and a dram is three-quarters of a teaspoon. You know what could have told me this? The Calculator app on my iPhone. If you’ve been using your calculator for years and wondering how on earth you missed this handy feature, it’s only been a thing since iOS 18 launched in 2024. So you haven’t been out of the loop for too long.
It’s easy, and you don’t need to download anything or update to a new version. Just follow these steps.
Yes! The Calculator also features a Math Notes section, which is similar to the regular Notes app but pulls double duty as a conversion calculator. Let’s say you want to make a note to yourself that 1 ounce equals roughly 28 grams. Click the Calculator icon in the upper right again, and this time, select Math Notes.
Give your note a heading, or just hit enter to start typing in the body of the Note. Type whatever you want to remember, such as “1 ounce to grams.” The Calculator will automatically convert it for you, as well as any other conversions you type, and keep a record of them for later.
Yes, and it’s kind of a big one. The Calculator conversion can’t convert weight to volume, which requires knowing the density of the product you’re measuring. In other words, it’s more math than a simple 1-to-1 conversion. So if you’re making bread and the recipe calls for 200 grams of flour, the Calculator converter will not give you the cups.
What it can do is convert weight to weight and volume to volume, as well as other measurements that share the same physical properties. But … you have your phone, right? One way to figure out how many cups of flour you need for that recipe is to use an ingredient-specific conversion chart, such as this one at King Arthur Baking Company.
Cooking conversions are a tiny sliver of what the Calculator can do. Need to change dollars to pesos for your upcoming trip to Puerto Vallarta? No problem. Running a 10K race and can’t remember how many miles that is? Pull up the Calculator. Other properties it can convert include energy (like calories to kilocalories), temperature (Celsius to Fahrenheit), time (minutes to hours) and tons of others.
Yes, but because Androids don’t have a single Calculator app like iPhones do, using it will depend on your device. On a Google Pixel, open the Calculator app and select “Unit Conversion.” Samsung Galaxy devices work the same way, but other Android devices may be slightly different. Keep in mind, though, that weight-to-volume limitations exist for both iPhones and Androids.

Picture it: You’re making holiday cookies, up to your elbows in flour and sugar and little red and green sprinkles, when your recipe throws you for a loop. In the old days, you might have just muddled through and hoped for the best, or searched the back of your cookbook for tips and tricks to solve whatever problem you’d encountered.

But now, you’re more likely to reach for your iPhone, which is probably what you’re using to follow the recipe anyway. iPhones have changed the way we cook and bake, and I can’t tell you how many times I’ve reached for mine to Google something mid-recipe. But what if you didn’t have to search the internet at all?

Good news: You don’t, at least for one particularly common cooking problem—because the answer is right on your phone. Ahead, I’ll tell you about a super handy iPhone feature that I had no idea existed until recently but is guaranteed to make my holiday cooking and yours so much easier.

Read on to learn about this secret iPhone feature, and get baking!

Get Reader’s Digest’s Read Up newsletter for more holidays, tech, travel, entertainment, humor and fun facts all week long.

What secret iPhone feature is a total game changer for holiday cooking?

It’s the Unit Conversion feature in your iPhone’s calculator, and it really helps. Need to know how many grams are in an ounce or how many pints there are in a quart? This little feature can tell you. Does your Nigella Lawson turkey recipe call for liters of brine instead of gallons? Grab your iPhone calculator and make that turkey with confidence.

I cook a lot, but aside from a handful of familiar conversions, like 3 teaspoons = 1 tablespoon, my brain just doesn’t have a lot of room for math-y minutiae. Just the other day, a recipe called for 8 tablespoons of water, and I got out a cup, filled it to the top and counted them out. Another wanted me to add a “dram” of flavoring, which might as well have been in a different language, not to mention from another century.

Little did I know that 8 tablespoons is a half-cup, and a dram is three-quarters of a teaspoon. You know what could have told me this? The Calculator app on my iPhone. If you’ve been using your calculator for years and wondering how on earth you missed this handy feature, it’s only been a thing since iOS 18 launched in 2024. So you haven’t been out of the loop for too long.

How do you use this feature?

It’s easy, and you don’t need to download anything or update to a new version. Just follow these steps.

  1. Open the Calculator by searching your home screen or looking in the Utilities folder.
  2. Click the Calculator icon in the upper right.
  3. Choose “Convert.” You will see two numerical fields, each labeled with a unit of measurement.
  4. Select each unit, one at a time, to choose the conversion (for example, ounces to grams).
  5. Click the checkmark to get back to the Calculator interface.
  6. Select the field you know (such as ounces) and type it in; the Calculator will convert it automatically (in the example above, from 1 ounce to 28.35 grams).

Is there another way to convert measurements in the Calculator?

Yes! The Calculator also features a Math Notes section, which is similar to the regular Notes app but pulls double duty as a conversion calculator. Let’s say you want to make a note to yourself that 1 ounce equals roughly 28 grams. Click the Calculator icon in the upper right again, and this time, select Math Notes.

Give your note a heading, or just hit enter to start typing in the body of the Note. Type whatever you want to remember, such as “1 ounce to grams.” The Calculator will automatically convert it for you, as well as any other conversions you type, and keep a record of them for later.

Does this miracle feature have any limitations?

Yes, and it’s kind of a big one. The Calculator conversion can’t convert weight to volume, which requires knowing the density of the product you’re measuring. In other words, it’s more math than a simple 1-to-1 conversion. So if you’re making bread and the recipe calls for 200 grams of flour, the Calculator converter will not give you the cups.

What it can do is convert weight to weight and volume to volume, as well as other measurements that share the same physical properties. But … you have your phone, right? One way to figure out how many cups of flour you need for that recipe is to use an ingredient-specific conversion chart, such as this one at King Arthur Baking Company.

What else can you do with this app?

Cooking conversions are a tiny sliver of what the Calculator can do. Need to change dollars to pesos for your upcoming trip to Puerto Vallarta? No problem. Running a 10K race and can’t remember how many miles that is? Pull up the Calculator. Other properties it can convert include energy (like calories to kilocalories), temperature (Celsius to Fahrenheit), time (minutes to hours) and tons of others.

Does a similar feature also exist on Androids?

Yes, but because Androids don’t have a single Calculator app like iPhones do, using it will depend on your device. On a Google Pixel, open the Calculator app and select “Unit Conversion.” Samsung Galaxy devices work the same way, but other Android devices may be slightly different. Keep in mind, though, that weight-to-volume limitations exist for both iPhones and Androids.

  • Google Support: “Use Google Calculator on your Pixel phone”
  • Samsung: “Use your Galaxy phone’s Calculator, Calendar, and Clock apps”
  • King Arthur Baking Company: “Ingredient weight chart”
